name: Nairobi National Museum
funding: National Museums of Kenya, a state corporation, runs it. Planet Africa (2024 to 2025) was funded by the German Research Foundation and Germany's Foreign Office.
watch: In May 2017 museum management pulled works by Michael Soi, Patrick Mukabi and Bertiers Mbatia on opening day, saying they were unsuitable for children.
records_note: No records of its own: parent National Museums of Kenya posts annual reports for 2015 to 2019 and names its board; no accounts or donors.
affiliations_note: Part of National Museums of Kenya, alongside Nairobi Gallery, Karen Blixen Museum and Fort Jesus Museum, and initiated in 1910 by the East Africa and Uganda Natural History Society.

overview: Kenya's main national museum on Museum Hill, Nairobi, run by National Museums of Kenya, a state corporation (Wikipedia).

Began in 1910 as a collection of the East African Natural History Society (now Nature Kenya). Construction at the present site started in 1929 and it opened on 22 September 1930 as the Coryndon Museum, named for Sir Robert Coryndon (The Standard; museum site). Renamed after independence (The Standard says 1963; Wikipedia says 1964).

Closed on 15 October 2005 for its first major rebuilding since 1930. Reopened on 14 July 2008, opened by President Mwai Kibaki (The Standard). Triad Architects Limited designed a visitors' centre as part of the master plan.

Permanent galleries: Cradle of Human Kind, Story of Mammals, History of Kenya, Cycles of Life and a numismatic exhibition (museum site). The grounds hold the Nairobi Snake Park, a botanic garden and a nature trail (Wikipedia).

Visiting: open daily 8:30am to 5:30pm, including weekends and public holidays. Night tours for booked groups of 10 or more (museum site). From 7 May 2026: Kenyan and East African adults KSh 350, children KSh 200. Rest of Africa $9 and $6. Outside Africa $18 and $9 (The Star).
details.funding_verdict: Nairobi National Museum: mainly public: Kenya's state corporation, with a European Union-funded rebuild and German project funding
funding: 2005 to 2008 renovation: Sh800 million from the European Union under the National Museums of Kenya Support Programme (The Standard, Wangeci Kanyeki, 2013).

Planet Africa, a travelling exhibition that opened in Nairobi on 29 November 2024 and ran until 31 May 2025 (blog post dated 29 January 2025): funded by the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft and the German Foreign Office; no amounts stated (German Archaeological Institute blog). Partners: University of Ghana, Museum fur Vor- und Fruhgeschichte Berlin and the Staatliche Museen zu Berlin.

red_flags.heading: State censorship, May 2017
points: May 2017: management of National Museums of Kenya, the state corporation that runs the museum, pulled works by Michael Soi, Patrick Mukabi and Bertiers Mbatia from an exhibition due to open on International Museum Day, whose theme was "Speaking the Unspeakable in Museums". Business Daily (Margaretta wa Gacheru, 18 May 2017) reports that the museum judged the art "inappropriate" for its main audience, school children, and that the artists were told the day before the opening.
Mukabi said the artists had been encouraged to make work in keeping with the theme. Curator Lydia Galavu said the art had been packed away (Business Daily).

press.overall: One critical report found, about the 2017 ban, in Kenyan press rather than the art press.

items.title: Margaretta wa Gacheru, "Museum bans works by three of Kenya's finest artists" (2017)
points: Calls the museum's position "contradictory to say the least" given the day's theme, and says the works were "censored by the management of the National Museums of Kenya"; on social media the decision was called "hypocritical".
Points to a breakdown in communication: the museum had asked all three artists to make work for the day.
Names National Museums of Kenya management; the museum's own response is limited to the child audience.

details.bottom_line: The money is Kenyan state funding, an EU-financed rebuild and German research and foreign office funds for one project, with no corporate sponsor named. The weak point is the 2017 removal of three artists' work on International Museum Day, with no reporting found of a reversal. Worth watching: whether National Museums of Kenya publishes recent accounts and a donor list.

name: Gapar Aitiev Kyrgyz National Museum of Fine Arts
watch: In December 2019 a Culture Ministry commission confiscated works from the Feminnale. Director Mira Dzhangaracheva left after death threats.
records_note: A state museum; a search found none from the ministry.

overview: National art museum on Sovietskaya Street, opposite the opera house and near Ala-Too Square in central Bishkek (SRAS Museum Studies Abroad).
Grew from a picture gallery the Kyrgyz regional Communist Party committee opened in 1934 (Voices on Central Asia). It opened in January 1935 with 72 works chosen by Semyon Chuikov (SRAS).
Named for Gapar Aitiev, an early Soviet Kyrgyz artist (SRAS).
The current building, a brutalist design by Shailo Djekshenbaev, opened in 1974 (SRAS).

Holds about 18,000 items, about 3,000 of them ethnographic, with Kyrgyz applied art (felt carpets, embroidery, silver jewellery, wood carving) the largest part, plus painting, graphics, sculpture and reproductions of European works (Voices on Central Asia; SRAS).

The permanent display closed for repairs from 27 September 2025, with no reopening date given (24.kg). Earlier visitors reported a low entry fee (20 som for students in 2018) and guided tours in Russian, Kyrgyz and English (SRAS).
details.funding_verdict: Gapar Aitiev Museum: public: Kyrgyzstan's Ministry of Culture
funding: Owned and run by the Ministry of Culture, Information, Sports and Youth Policy (SRAS); the culture minister appoints and removes its director (24.kg).
A 2022 visitor wrote that the old building "does not seem to have the facilities to keep its art in good condition", with damaged frames and works stored haphazardly (SRAS).

red_flags.heading: Feminnale censorship by the Culture Ministry
points: The first Feminnale of contemporary art, with 56 artists from 22 countries, opened at the museum in late November 2019 (Human Rights Watch gives 28 November; New East Digital Archive).

Culture Minister Azamat Zhamankulov met its opponents and ordered several works he called "provocative" and "amoral" removed (Human Rights Watch), including, in the New East Digital Archive's account, Zoya Falkova's punching bag shaped like a female body; the Danish artist Julie Savery's performance involving nudity was cancelled (ArtReview).

On 2 December the minister said that "under the flag of feminism, campaigns with a naked woman were held in Parliament and in a church" and that a dedicated panel would review the exhibition (24.kg). On 5 December MP Kurmankul Zulushev called for a police investigation of some works (Human Rights Watch).

red_flags.heading: Threats and the director's departure
points: Director Mira Dzhangaracheva left after threats against her and her staff, including a threat to "tear me apart, to rape me" (Human Rights Watch). The ministry said she was dismissed; she said she stepped down voluntarily (24.kg; ArtReview).

She blamed the nationalist group Kyrk Choro, whose supporters objected to the show (Voices on Central Asia). On 6 December 2019 the government announced an investigation into the threats (Human Rights Watch).
The ministry appointed deputy director and chief curator Aigul Mambetkazieva in her place; the Union of Artists asked for Dzhangaracheva's return (24.kg).

press.overall: The coverage criticises the government's censorship and the nationalist campaign, not the museum's own conduct.

items.title: Taylor Dafoe, "Kyrgyzstan Censored a Feminist Art Show at the National Museum of Fine Arts. Now Its Director Has Resigned" (2019)
points: Per excerpts, reports that officials removed works, including Zoya Falkova's punching-bag sculpture, and that the culture minister said Dzhangaracheva had been relieved of her duties while she said she resigned.

items.title: Hillary Margolis, "Feminist Art Exhibit Threatened in Kyrgyzstan" (2019)
points: Argues the government should protect the artists and organisers and uphold free expression instead of limiting access to the art.
A human rights organisation, not art media.

details.bottom_line: The museum is paid for and controlled by the Kyrgyz state, with no private funders on record. The weak point is that control: in 2019 the culture minister removed works from a feminist show and the director left under threats. Worth watching: when the permanent display reopens and who pays for the repairs.

name: Cráter Invertido
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.
highlight: A cooperative in Mexico City, active since 2011, that self-manages a house-workshop with a risographic printing press and an experimental radio station.

overview: Artist cooperative that self-manages a multidisciplinary house-workshop in Mexico City, with a risograph press and an experimental radio (stated by the space and by Arts Collaboratory).

Since 2011 the cooperative has been made up of graduates of the National School of Visual Arts (UNAM) and the "La Esmeralda" School of Painting, Sculpture and Printmaking (INBA) (MUAC, UNAM). Time Out Mexico (2016) says the group came together at La Esmeralda under the name Grupo D.
Publishes risograph-printed work through its own imprint, Cráneo Invertido (MUAC, UNAM).
Time Out Mexico (review of February 2016) gave the address as Joaquín García Icazbalceta 32, colonia San Rafael, near Metro San Cosme.

Programmes listed on its site: Casita, Radio Tropiezo, Imaginarios and Taller XD. It also takes part in decentralised processes on the care and defence of territories, biodiversity, shared learning and commonality (Arts Collaboratory).
Took part in the 56th Venice Biennale (2015), the Jakarta Biennale (2015), Sonsbeek '16, the Gwangju Biennale (2016) and the Conundrum of Imagination in Vienna (2017) (Arts Collaboratory).
Visiting: Time Out Mexico (2016) listed free entry and opening by appointment, depending on the event.
details.funding_verdict: Cráter Invertido: member-run cooperative and member of the Arts Collaboratory network, which Hivos and DOEN Foundation started
funding: Arts Collaboratory lists Cooperativa Cráter Invertido among its 25 member organisations. DOEN Foundation is also a member and says it contributes to the network "through its funding, its network and its knowledge" (Arts Collaboratory).

Wikipedia says Arts Collaboratory was established in 2007 by the Dutch organisations Hivos and DOEN Foundation and is implemented in collaboration with the Mondriaan Foundation. It gives long-term support to independent visual arts organisations in Africa, Asia and Latin America, plus project funds of up to 15,000 euros per project.
details.bottom_line: Cráter Invertido is a member-run artist cooperative and a member of the Arts Collaboratory network, which the Dutch organisations Hivos and DOEN Foundation started in 2007 to support independent visual arts organisations in Africa, Asia and Latin America.

name: Museo de la Ciudad de México
funding: Public museum run by the Mexico City Ministry of Culture.
watch: In April 2025 seven people protested outside against Fabián Cháirez's show; a federal judge then suspended it after religious groups' amparo suit.
why_flagged: Public museum run by the Mexico City Ministry of Culture.
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.
records_note: The ministry publishes ministry-wide Glosa reports for 2019 to 2023.

overview: City history museum at Pino Suárez 30 in the Centro Histórico, three blocks from the Zócalo, in the former Palacio de los Condes de Santiago de Calimaya (Spanish Wikipedia).

The land went from Hernán Cortés to Juan Gutiérrez Altamirano. The palace was rebuilt between 1776 and 1779 by Francisco Antonio de Guerrero y Torres in Baroque style. It was declared national heritage in 1931 (Spanish Wikipedia).

The family that owned it lived there until 1964. After the building was expropriated they sold it to the city government (Spanish Wikipedia). It had become a vecindad with businesses on the first floor (Chilango).

In 1960 the Departamento del Distrito Federal decreed it the seat of the official museum of Mexico City. Pedro Ramírez Vázquez remodelled it and the museum was inaugurated on 31 October 1964 (Spanish Wikipedia).

On site: temporary exhibitions, a permanent studio of painter Joaquín Clausell, a 1923 cargo truck and viceregal carriages, the Biblioteca Jaime Torres Bodet and a Fondo de Cultura Económica bookshop. Concerts, dance, theatre, workshops and talks (Chilango, Montse Quintana, 21 February 2023).
Visiting: Tuesday to Sunday 10:00 to 18:00, general admission 38 pesos (Chilango, February 2023).
details.funding_verdict: Museo de la Ciudad de México: mainly public: Mexico City government through its Secretaría de Cultura
funding: The venue belongs to the Secretaría de Cultura de la Ciudad de México, with the city government as administrator (Spanish Wikipedia).

The city culture secretary, Ana Francis Mor, said at the April 2025 reopening of the Cháirez show: "no podemos permitir la censura nunca" (translated: we can never allow censorship) (El Financiero, 17 April 2025).

red_flags.heading: Protest outside the museum and court suspension of an exhibition
points: Fabián Cháirez's show "La segunda venida del Señor", nine oil paintings made between 2018 and 2023, opened at the museum on 2 April 2025 for a run to 30 April (El Financiero, 17 April 2025; Vanguardia, 17 April 2025).

Seven people protested outside the museum with the slogan "No ofendas mi fe, en nombre del arte" (Vanguardia, Mauro Marines, "En plena Semana Santa vuelven a suspender la exposición de Fabián Cháirez", 17 April 2025). El Financiero reported that Catholic groups had protested outside UNAM's Academia de San Carlos in February 2025 and that protests had returned.

Religious groups filed an amparo suit on 15 April 2025, saying the show violates freedom of worship; the Juzgado Sexto de Distrito en Materia Administrativa granted a provisional suspension, notified to the museum on 15 April (Vanguardia). UnoTV calls the plaintiffs "un reducido grupo de ciudadanos" (a small group of citizens).
The Asociación de Abogados Cristianos had earlier brought more than 30 amparos that led to the show's removal from the Academia de San Carlos in February 2025 (Vanguardia).

The judge ordered a definitive suspension, reported on 28 and 29 April 2025, and the museum complied and removed the exhibition (UnoTV, 29 April 2025; La Razón, Julio Vázquez, "Suspenden definitivamente exposición de Fabián Cháirez en el Museo de la Ciudad de México", 29 April 2025).

The city Secretaría de Cultura announced the provisional suspension and reaffirmed its commitment to artistic freedom of expression (Vanguardia). After the definitive order it said it would take steps to defend the right of access to culture, and called the ban a "retroceso" (setback, translated) in building a plural and democratic society (UnoTV; La Razón).
The suit and the court order came from outside the museum and the city government. The court, not the city government, ordered the closure, and the city culture ministry opposed it.

details.bottom_line: The museum is a public institution of the Mexico City government, run through its Secretaría de Cultura. In April 2025 seven people protested outside it and religious groups won a court suspension of the Cháirez exhibition, which the city culture ministry opposed.

name: Museo de los Pintores Oaxaqueños
funding: State museum run by the Oaxaca state patronato for cultural and tourist units.
watch: Temporary exhibitions only, no permanent collection. The state government began rehabilitating the colonial building.
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.

overview: Museum of Oaxacan art (MUPO) on Avenida de la Independencia in the historic centre of Oaxaca de Juárez, at the corner of García Vigil street (Oaxaca Lending Library kiosk; Spanish Wikipedia).
Opened as a museum in 2003 (the Spanish Wikipedia infobox says 2003, its introduction says 2004).

The colonial building opened on 26 January 1686 as the Colegio de las Doncellas de Nuestra Señora de la Presentación, paid for by the priest Juan Gómez de Tapia and the philanthropist Miguel Fernández Fiallo to educate girls who lacked access to schooling (Spanish Wikipedia).

Later uses: the first seat of the Museo Nacional de Antropología e Historia in 1933, the State Regional Museum until 1986, the City Council until 1992 and the state Secretaría de Turismo from 1993 to 2003 (Spanish Wikipedia; Oaxaca Lending Library kiosk).

The museum has no permanent collection and four temporary exhibition rooms named for Rufino Tamayo, Rodolfo Morales, Rodolfo Nieto and Francisco Gutiérrez. Activities include dance classes, guided tours, lectures, book presentations and educational services (Spanish Wikipedia).
The museum states its aim as promoting and developing the visual arts in Oaxaca and beyond, with a focus on conserving, analysing and sharing works made in Oaxaca (Oaxaca Lending Library kiosk).
Visiting: Tuesday to Sunday, 10:00 to 18:00 (Spanish Wikipedia).
details.funding_verdict: Museo de los Pintores Oaxaqueños: mainly public: Oaxaca state government
funding: It is run by the Patronato de las Unidades de Servicios Culturales y Turísticos del Estado de Oaxaca, and the state government started the renovation that adapted the building for art exhibitions (Spanish Wikipedia).

In May 2025 the Secretaría de las Culturas y Artes (Seculta), headed by Flavio Sosa Villavicencio, and the Instituto del Patrimonio Cultural del Estado de Oaxaca (Inpac) began intervention works at state cultural spaces including MUPO, covering facades, doors and windows, signage, accessibility, electrical systems and civil protection (Excélsior, Patricia Briseño, 30 May 2025).
details.bottom_line: The museum is a state institution of Oaxaca housed in a 1686 colonial building, run by the state's cultural and tourist services patronage and maintained by the state government through Seculta and Inpac. The money documented is state money.

name: Museo Nacional de Historia, Castillo de Chapultepec
funding: Federal: the museum's site is hosted by the Instituto Nacional de Antropología e Historia (INAH) and carries the federal government logo. The pages read did not state a budget or sponsors.
watch: National history museum in the castle built in 1785 to 1787 as a viceroy's retreat, later a military academy and Maximilian and Carlota's residence; it opened as a museum in September 1944 (INAH).
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.
records_note: The pages read did not show published accounts.

overview: Museo Nacional de Historia is in the Castillo de Chapultepec in Chapultepec Forest, Mexico City (INAH).
The castle was built in 1785 to 1787 on the order of Viceroy Bernardo de Gálvez; in 1939 President Lázaro Cárdenas decreed it a museum, which opened in September 1944 (INAH).

What is there: collections and artefacts of figures in Mexican history; the site lists history halls, Alcázar halls, murals, archaeology and the history of Chapultepec, and a gigapixel section (INAH). The pages read gave no object count.
Archive: the site menu lists a library (Biblioteca); the pages read did not give holdings.
details.funding_verdict: Museo Nacional de Historia: federal, run through INAH
funding: INAH (federal): the museum site is on the INAH domain and shows the Mexican government logo.
No reporting found, in the pages read, of sponsors, donor gifts or the INAH disputes named in the brief.
details.bottom_line: A federal museum paid from the INAH budget as far as the pages read show; no amounts or disputes were found.

name: Museo Universitario del Chopo
watch: Sol Henaro has directed it since 2024. A Juan Gabriel show due 28 May 2026 was postponed with no reason given.
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.
records_note: Owner UNAM posts audited accounts for 2022 to 2025 and names its governing boards.
affiliations_note: A UNAM museum listed under the university's Coordinación de Difusión Cultural beside MUAC and Museo Experimental El Eco.

overview: Contemporary art and culture museum of the Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México (UNAM) in the Santa María la Ribera neighbourhood of Mexico City, under UNAM's Coordinación de Difusión Cultural (Spanish Wikipedia).
Opened as a university museum on 25 November 1975 (Spanish Wikipedia; Rafael Paz, Gaceta UNAM, 21 August 2025, on its 50th anniversary).

The building, known as El Chopo, is a prefabricated Jugendstil iron-and-glass structure designed by Bruno Möhring, first used at a 1902 exhibition in Düsseldorf, and assembled in Santa María la Ribera between 1901 and 1905 by the engineer Luis Bacmeister for the entrepreneur José Landero y Coss (Spanish Wikipedia).

The building housed the Museo Nacional de Historia Natural from 1913 and joined UNAM in 1929. After the natural history museum closed in 1964 it stood abandoned, and a 1970 plan to sell its iron was stopped by its monument status. UNAM restored it from 1973 (Spanish Wikipedia).
It closed in October 2005 for a redesign by the architect Enrique Norten and reopened on 18 May 2010 (Spanish Wikipedia).

On site: galleries, the Foro del Dinosaurio Juan José Gurrola, a documentation centre, the Café del Chopo and an auditorium, with exhibitions, music, dance, theatre, film and low-cost workshops (Spanish Wikipedia). The Tianguis Cultural del Chopo began inside the museum on 4 October 1980 and now meets on Saturdays on Juan Aldama. It was recognised as intangible cultural heritage of Mexico City in 2023 (Gaceta UNAM). The Festival Internacional de Diversidad Sexual grew from a Semana Cultural Lésbica Gay begun in 1987 (Gaceta UNAM).

Sol Henaro Palomino has directed it since January 2024 (UNAM 2024 report), and calls it "un centro social travestido de museo" (a social centre disguised as a museum; translation; Gaceta UNAM, 21 August 2025).

In May 2026 the Juan Gabriel exhibition "Un lugar de ambiente. Legado y disidencia", organised with the 39th Festival Internacional por la Diversidad Sexual, was due to open on 28 May (Roberto Frías, Gaceta UNAM, 25 May 2026). The museum cancelled the opening that day, postponing it "hasta nuevo aviso" (Eduardo Alavez, Chilango, 29 May 2026), then opened to the public hours later and held the official inauguration on 13 June. The show runs to 28 August (Frida Juárez Bautista, El Universal, 19 June 2026).

Henaro told El Universal that the delay was an administrative matter to settle with the artist's representatives. Unverified: social media users said it was a copyright problem, as reported by El Universal, which says the reasons "siguen sin esclarecerse" (remain unclear; translation).
details.funding_verdict: Museo Universitario del Chopo: mainly public: UNAM, itself funded by the federal government
funding: The museum belongs to UNAM, a public university. UNAM's 2026 budget is 59,878 million pesos, of which 53,749 million (89.8%) is federal subsidy and 6,129 million (10.2%) is the university's own income (Mirtha Hernández, Gaceta UNAM, 12 February 2026).
UNAM's 2024 annual report describes the museum's programme under Henaro, including two new exhibition spaces, El Gabinete for emerging artists and an outdoor space for interventions.
details.bottom_line: The money behind the museum is UNAM's budget, about 90% federal subsidy in 2026. The documented episode is the cancelled and then reinstated opening of the Juan Gabriel show in May 2026, for which the museum gave an administrative reason.

name: Zanabazar Museum of Fine Art
funding: Mongolian state museum (founded 1966) listed by the National Centre for Cultural Heritage; UNESCO preservation partner.
records_note: Its own site is down; parent body NCCH posts activity reports for 2006 to 2022 but no accounts, funders or board.
affiliations_note: A Mongolian state museum listed under the National Centre for Cultural Heritage; no network, branch or partner museum is named. Member of ASEMUS.

overview: Museum of Mongolian fine art in Chingeltei District, Ulaanbaatar (Wikipedia). Google Arts & Culture gives the address as Sambuu St, CHD 4th khoroo, Ulaanbaatar 15170. The postal address in the footer of the National Centre for Cultural Heritage (NCCH) page is Khan-Uul district, 21st khoroo, Buyant-Ukhaa 2, the centre's own address.
Galleries: 12 according to Wikipedia and Google Arts & Culture, 10 exhibition halls according to the NCCH page, covering Mongolian art from ancient times to the early 20th century (NCCH).
Founded in 1966 (NCCH). Wikipedia says it was proposed in 1965 by the chairman of the Mongolian Craftsmen's Union Committee and opened to the public on 23 July 1966.
Named in 1995 for Gombodorj Zanabazar, the sculptor whose works it holds, including Sita Tara statues, the Five Dhyani Buddhas and the Bodhi Stupa (Google Arts & Culture).
Building: a Russian merchant built it in 1905 and it was later used as a bank (Wikipedia).

Collection: nearly 16,600 objects according to Google Arts & Culture, more than 16,000 according to the NCCH page, and more than 20,000 according to Wikipedia, which names paintings by Marzan Sharav. The museum joined Google Arts & Culture in 2015 with a virtual tour (Wikipedia).
Since 2004 it has run a UNESCO project, "Development of Museums and Protection of Nomadic Cultural Heritage" (Wikipedia).
Visiting: the NCCH page lists hours of Monday to Friday, 08:30 to 17:30.

Neighbouring tower: the museum sued the Capital City Urban Planning and General Master Plan Office over its approval of a 28-storey office and banking building planned by Trade and Development Bank beside the museum. The museum argued that groundwater could cause settlement that cracks its building, that the tower would stand three metres from its protected zone, and that no measures were planned to protect the heritage building. The first-instance court dismissed the claim, the appeal court left that ruling in place, and on 2 December 2025 the Supreme Court upheld both rulings (iKon.mn, G. Mörön, 4 December 2025, title translated: "Court dismisses three-tier lawsuit opposing 28-storey building near the G. Zanabazar Museum of Fine Arts").
details.funding_verdict: Zanabazar Museum of Fine Art: listed on the website of the National Centre for Cultural Heritage; UNESCO project since 2004
funding: The NCCH site (ncch.gov.mn) carries a page for the museum with hours, contact details and a description of its collection.
UNESCO project since 2004 on museum development and the protection of nomadic cultural heritage (Wikipedia).
details.bottom_line: The museum was founded in 1966, is listed on the National Centre for Cultural Heritage site and has run a UNESCO project since 2004 (Wikipedia). Its lawsuit over the neighbouring Trade and Development Bank tower was dismissed at three court levels, the last on 2 December 2025 (iKon.mn).

name: Fondation Ifitry
funding: Run under Maroc Premium Foundation, which has overseen the Casablanca Biennale and the Essaouira art centre since 2014.
watch: Artist residency near Essaouira founded in 2008 by Mostapha Romli.
records_note: Its parent biennale shows 2021 partner logos without names, with no reports, accounts or board.
affiliations_note: Part of the Maroc Premium Foundation, which also oversees the Essaouira art centre, the Casablanca International Biennale and the BIC Project Space.

overview: Artists' residency on the coastal road between Essaouira and Safi, about 50 km from Essaouira and 70 km from Safi, directly opposite the Contemporary Art Centre (Casablanca Biennale website).

Created in 2008 by Mostapha Romli and made a foundation in 2014 (The Art Newspaper France, Olivier Rachet, 3 August 2022). The Casablanca Biennale website describes Romli as a Moroccan artist, photographer and publisher who initiated the Biennale in 2012.

Facilities: twelve ocean-facing pavilions of 20 to 120 m2 with one to three bedrooms, and workshops for engraving, screen printing, painting, ceramics, photography and video (Casablanca Biennale website).

The pavilions are described as an extension of the Contemporary Art Centre of Essaouira (Casablanca Biennale website), whose collection holds about 2,000 works by Moroccan and other artists (The Art Newspaper France, 2022).
Artists reach the residency by applying to a selection committee or by invitation for exhibition projects, according to Romli (The Art Newspaper France, 2022).
By 2022 it had hosted more than 570 artists from 73 countries. By January 2014 the count was 374 artists from 45 countries (The Art Newspaper France, 2022; Le360, Bouthaina Azami, 25 January 2014).

Since 2014 the Casablanca Biennale has operated under the aegis of the Maroc Premium Foundation, which also oversees a contemporary art center established in 2011, a collection of contemporary works and the BIC Project Space in Casablanca, opened in 2019 (Casablanca Biennale website).
The 6th Casablanca Biennale, conceived by the curator Marisa Caichiolo, runs from 10 December 2026 to 10 January 2027 in Essaouira and cites the Ifitry residency (Casablanca Biennale website).
details.funding_verdict: Fondation Ifitry: founded by the artist Mostapha Romli; artists donate works made during their stay to support it
funding: Some artists donated works made during their stay at the residency to support the foundation (Le360, Bouthaina Azami, "Naissance d'une fondation, une exposition exceptionnelle", 25 January 2014).

The same Le360 article describes a collective show of works made at Ifitry at the Sofitel Casablanca Tour Blanche, part of an exhibition cycle started by Maroc Premium and Sofitel Luxury Hotels (Le360, 2014).
details.bottom_line: Fondation Ifitry is the artists' residency created by Mostapha Romli in 2008. Its documented support is works donated by artists in 2014 and a collective show at a Casablanca hotel within an exhibition cycle started by Maroc Premium and Sofitel Luxury Hotels. The Casablanca Biennale that Romli initiated operates under the Maroc Premium Foundation.

name: Montresso Art Foundation (Jardin Rouge)
watch: Residency on a 10-hectare olive grove 20 km outside Marrakech, hosting about 40 artists a year; visits by appointment.
tier_note: No reason for the flag is recorded.
records_note: It names only collaborating institutions and its Amis de Jardin Rouge association.
affiliations_note: Works with the Musée Mohammed VI in Rabat and runs its education programme through the friends association Les Amis de Jardin Rouge.

overview: Artist residency and art space among olive groves in a small village about twenty kilometres from Marrakech, run by the Montresso Art Foundation, which says it has been settled in Morocco since 2009 (Rivet).
A private initiative of the French art collector and patron Jean-Louis Haguenauer, who bought the land in 2002. Jardin Rouge opened in 2009 (Arterritory, Una Meistere, 16 February 2020).
On site: eight artists' studios. About thirty artists of various nationalities are hosted each year, and eighty had been hosted in total by the time of the February 2020 interview (Arterritory).
The residency is open to painters, photographers and sculptors from anywhere in the world. Stays last from one month to 90 days (ONArt, 20 November 2022).

Selected artists get accommodation, meals, an individual workshop, equipment and transport. In agreement with the artist, a selection of works made during the residency is offered for purchase (TransArtists).
Visits are by appointment (Arterritory, TransArtists).
details.funding_verdict: Montresso Art Foundation (Jardin Rouge): private: a private initiative of the collector Jean-Louis Haguenauer
funding: The foundation funds the production of the artistic project approved by the selection committee and covers transport, individual accommodation, meals, equipment and an individual workshop (TransArtists); ONArt says the foundation finances the artist's production.
Jardin Rouge is described as a private initiative of Haguenauer (Arterritory).
details.bottom_line: Montresso is a private initiative of the collector Jean-Louis Haguenauer, who bought the land in 2002 and opened Jardin Rouge in 2009, according to Arterritory. The foundation pays for residents' production, transport, accommodation and meals.
